catalog_quote: This chapter discusses aspects of prosody in SuNdaLa, specifically tone and reduplication. ... Tone assignment in nouns is unpredictable and has therefore to be lexically marked.Verbs show purely accentual properties as there is always one high tone in a construction which is assigned in one position (either the penultimate or antepenultimate mora). ... The tone system of verbs in SuNdaLa is fundamentally different from that of nominals.While for nouns the assignment of high tones is not predictable, it is predictable for verbs; thus the tone system of verbs has characteristics of an accentual rather than a pure tone system. ... Like in most other Bantu languages the presence of H tones in SuNdaLa is also determined largely by tense morphemes. sweep_summary: Ndali (ndal1241) is in the catalog as tonal on Mtenje 2016 (UCT PhD, open, on file). Of the 21 sweep titles, 20 are Glottolog keyword misassignments (papers on English, Korean, Chinese, Old English, German, theory) triggered by the word 'prosodically'; only Botne 1998 (SAL 27(1), open, already on file) is about Ndali. Read in full: it treats Chindali prominence as high tone '(accent)' with mora-counted vowel shortening, speculates tone is 'becoming more stress-like', and posits no word-stress rule, so it confirms the tonal coding without superseding Mtenje 2016. Hyman 2009 (on file) cites Ndali once, silent on stress (its Ndali line is on printed p.205, not p.204 as the 9/16 row says). New this sweep: Botne 2008 Grammatical Sketch of Chindali now has chapter DOIs at degruyterbrill.com (Part 1: Phonology pp.5-16, doi:10.70249/9780871693037-005); access could not be confirmed (HTTP 202 empty body, no Crossref license), high priority to acquire. Mtenje 2006 'Tone in Cindali' (Lingua) is closed (no OA copy, abstract withheld); Kabuje 1995 (UDSM MA) not located; the Botne & Schafer 2008 dictionary is an archive.org lending copy only. Google Books API quota exhausted; all probes and records with.

new_statements.reading: First-hand description of Malawian Chindali by a field linguist: word-level prominence is lexical high tone (which Botne glosses as 'accent'), with vowel length governed by mora count and by the presence of a prefix H; 'penultimate prominence' is invoked only as a diachronic Bantu preference, and no synchronic word-stress rule is stated. This confirms the catalog's TONAL-OR-PITCH-ACCENT coding and adds nothing that would license a stress rule.

One caution for anyone reusing the p.117 fragment: 'tone-becoming more stress-like in nature-may be in the process of replacing moraic stem count' is a speculative diachronic aside about the conditioning of vowel shortening, not a statement that Chindali has word stress; the paper states no synchronic stress rule anywhere.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: all fragments of the deciding quotation are verbatim in the held extracted text of Mtenje 2016 at the stated printed pages (p.103 section 4.0, p.128 section 4.1.2.2), and the thesis contains no word-stress statement for Cindali (grep 'stress' returns only generic/lit items). The deciding source is a 2016 PhD with a dedicated prosody chapter on the author's own Cindali data, building on the two senior primaries (Botne 2008 APS sketch; Mtenje 2006 Lingua tone paper), which it reports as describing the same two-level tone system with lexical nominal tone and morphologically placed, accent-like verbal H. Botne 1998 (open, fetched sources now to independently glosses Chindali H as '(accent)' and frames prominence in tonal/moraic terms, confirming the TONAL-OR-PITCH-ACCENT coding; Hyman 2009 is silent. No word-stress rule is posited or denied.

sources.locator: p.97 (abstract), p.106 n.5, p.117 (section 11), p.120 (section 13); PDF pp.1, 10, 21, 24
sources.note: The only sweep item genuinely about Ndali. Describes Malawian Chindali noun prosody entirely in terms of high tone and mora count: prefix-vowel shortening is blocked by a high tone on the prefix, which Botne glosses as '(accent)'; he speculates that tone is 'becoming more stress-like' and invokes a diachronic Bantu 'preference for penultimate prominence', but posits no word-stress rule and marks lexical H tones throughout. Confirms the catalog's TONAL-OR-PITCH-ACCENT coding (lexical tone in nouns).
